subject: system-design
title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
summary: Quick order-of-magnitude math that sizes a system in your head — enough to justify a design choice without a spreadsheet.

blocks.text: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is rough arithmetic to size a system before you build it. The aim isn't a precise number — it's the order of magnitude, enough to know whether you need one server or a thousand, gigabytes or petabytes.
A handful of quantities tell you most of what a design must handle. Each follows from a daily action count and a per-item size.

items: QPS — derive from daily actions divided by seconds in a day.
Storage — object size multiplied by volume multiplied by retention.
Bandwidth — QPS multiplied by payload size.
Memory — what a cache must hold, often the hot fraction of total data.
1 day is about 86,400 seconds — round to 100k to keep the math easy.
Read/write ratios are often 10:1 or higher; design for reads first.
Latency: memory ~100 ns, SSD read ~100 us, disk seek ~10 ms.
A round trip within the same datacenter is ~0.5 ms.

blocks.text: Say a service takes 100M writes per day. Divide by ~100k seconds and you get roughly 1,150 writes per second on average. Traffic is never flat, so multiply by 2-3 for the peak — call it ~3,000 writes per second to provision for. From there, multiply by payload size for bandwidth and by retention for storage.

blocks.title: Round numbers, stated assumptions
blocks.text: Precision is a trap. Round aggressively and say your assumptions out loud — '100M writes a day, 1KB each, kept a year' — so the math is checkable and the conclusion is what matters.

These numbers justify design choices on the spot. If storage lands in the petabytes you reach for object storage and partitioning; if it's a few gigabytes a single node is fine. The estimate turns a vague 'it should scale' into a concrete decision.
